planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring as soon as soil is workable; remove first-year flowers to build a strong root system.

directions: Sonata is a Dutch-bred (a cross of Elsanta and Polka) mid-season June-bearer that has become a mainstay of European commercial strawberry production for its heavy, reliable cropping and good fruit firmness. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil and keep moisture consistent through flowering and fruit swell, since uneven watering is the main cause of misshapen fruit in this variety. The large, glossy berries hold their shape and sweetness well in cool, humid growing conditions, making it a dependable choice for matted-row home plantings as well as market growers.

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring; Malwina ripens very late, extending the June-bearing season well past most other cultivars.

directions: Malwina is a German-bred (by Peter Stoppel) late-season strawberry known for stretching the harvest window well beyond earlier June-bearers, with deep red, highly aromatic fruit that holds flavor even in warm late-season conditions. Its unusually tough skin and firm flesh give it better resistance to slug damage and fruit rot than many thinner-skinned varieties, and it tolerates brief dry spells better than most strawberries once established. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture during fruiting, and plan on it bearing roughly a week or two after standard mid-season types finish.

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring; valued as a late-season extender for U-pick and roadside plantings.

directions: AC Valley Sunset is a June-bearer bred by Andrew Jamieson at the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada research centre in Kentville, Nova Scotia, developed to carry a farm's picking season into its final weeks. It holds fruit size and quality later into the harvest than most comparable cultivars, which makes it a favorite for extending U-pick and farm-stand sales. Grow in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil with even irrigation, and expect it to fruit toward the tail end of the regular strawberry season rather than as an everbearer.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked.

directions: Imara is a Dutch-bred (Advanced Berry Breeding) primocane (fall-fruiting) red raspberry noted for vigorous, easy-to-manage canes and a heavy, uniform crop of large, firm berries that detach cleanly when ripe, speeding up hand harvest. It begins fruiting a bit earlier in the primocane season than many comparable cultivars, giving growers a longer fall picking window. For a single large fall crop, mow all canes to the ground in late winter; plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and irrigate during fruit development for best size and flavor.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in spring; ripens around the same time as other summer-fruiting black raspberries.

directions: Tahi, bred in Auckland, New Zealand by Shekinah Berry, is notable as the first entirely spineless black raspberry cultivar, removing one of the biggest deterrents to picking and pruning this richly flavored fruit; its name means "one" in Maori, a nod to that first-of-its-kind status. The upright, vigorous canes carry larger berries than older thorny black raspberry types, with the deep black color and intense, wine-like flavor typical of Rubus occidentalis. Grow in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and manage it like other black raspberries by tipping primocanes in summer to encourage branching and removing spent floricanes after harvest.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked.

directions: Brandywine was bred at the Geneva, New York experiment station (tested as NY905, released 1982), placing it in the purple raspberry class alongside other Geneva-program purple raspberries of that era. The reddish-purple, large, firm fruit carries a concentrated, tart-sweet flavor and holds together well under heat, making it a favorite for jam, jelly, and syrup rather than only fresh eating. The tall, vigorous canes tolerate the humid summers of the Northeast better than many red raspberries; grow in full sun with sturdy trellising and prune spent floricanes after harvest to keep the planting productive.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic soil; amend with sulfur or peat moss before planting if soil pH is above 5.5.

directions: Top Shelf is a patented northern highbush blueberry bred by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery and selected for exceptionally large, jumbo-sized, sky-blue berries on a strong, upright, easy-to-prune bush. It ripens a few weeks later than Duke, giving growers an additional late-season harvest window, and its vigor and heavy early yields make it attractive for both commercial blocks and home plantings. Grow in full sun in well-drained, strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5), mulch with pine bark or sawdust, and water consistently through fruit development since the large fruit size demands steady moisture.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic soil; amend with sulfur or peat moss before planting if soil pH is above 5.5.

directions: Bonus arose as a chance sport of the Elliott blueberry found in southwest Michigan and lives up to its name with some of the largest fruit of any highbush blueberry, with berries so big that it takes only around a hundred to make a pound. The mild, sweet flavor and striking fruit size make it a standout for U-pick operations, even though yields run a bit lighter than more productive modern cultivars. Grow in full sun in moist, well-drained, acidic soil; while self-fruitful, planting a cross-pollinating cultivar nearby improves both yield and berry size.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic soil; amend with sulfur or peat moss before planting if soil pH is above 5.5.

directions: Nelson is a Michigan-bred cross of Bluecrop and Berkeley that has become a dependable late-season highbush standby, producing large, firm, dark blue berries with a tangy-sweet flavor well after the main midseason flush finishes. The bush is vigorous and upright, tolerates a range of soil conditions better than some finicky cultivars, and stores and ships well thanks to its firm texture. Grow in full sun in consistently moist, acidic soil, and expect it to extend the picking season into late summer alongside other late cultivars like Elliott.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Amish Red (sometimes sold simply as Amish) is an American heirloom gooseberry valued for medium-sized, deep red berries with a sweet-tart, complex flavor and crisp texture unusual among older gooseberry types. It shows notably good resistance to both white pine blister rust and powdery mildew, two problems that plague many older gooseberry varieties, making it a sturdier choice for home orchards in humid regions. Plant in partial shade with cool, moist, humus-rich soil, prune to an open framework to ease picking among the thorny stems, and expect ripening in early-to-mid summer.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Black September is an old European black currant selection prized for ripening later than most black currant cultivars, with large, firm berries that are notably sweeter and less sharply acidic than typical blackcurrant flavor. That later ripening window and mellower taste make it well suited to fresh eating as well as the usual jams, syrups, and cordials. Grow in full sun to light shade in moist, fertile soil, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune out the oldest third of stems each winter to keep the bush productive, since it fruits best on younger wood.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; pair with a different, compatible-blooming cultivar nearby since Blue Hokkaido is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Blue Hokkaido is a Japanese-type honeyberry popular for its upright habit and large, sweet-tart, crisp berries, ripening later in the season than many early-blooming haskap cultivars. Pair it with another Japanese-type cultivar blooming at a similar time for reliable cross-pollination, since it is not consistently self-fruitful. Like other honeyberries it tolerates extreme winter cold and prefers cool-summer climates, performing best in full sun with moist, well-drained soil and struggling in hot, humid regions.
